intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that dystonia-25 (DYT25) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNAL gene (139312) on chromosome 18p11.

paragraphs.text: Dystonia-25 is an autosomal dominant form of primary torsion dystonia in which dystonia is the only neurologic sign. Fuchs et al. (2013) described the phenotype in GNAL mutation carriers as mainly cervical dystonia. Age at onset varied widely, and in over half of carriers the dystonia spread to other muscles, especially the facial muscles. Speech involvement was also common.

paragraphs.text: Bressman et al. (1994) examined 53 individuals from 4 generations of a non-Jewish North American family with adult-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia. Seven family members were affected, with a mean age at onset of 28.4 years (range, 7 to 50 years). In 6 of the 7, the neck was affected first. All 7 developed cervical dystonia, and 5 had dysarthria or dysphonia.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) studied 28 individuals with definite dystonia and complete clinical information from 8 multiplex families with primary torsion dystonia and GNAL mutations. All carriers were Caucasian of mixed European ancestry; one family (family P) had mixed Russian and Swiss Mennonite heritage. Families D1, P, and S had been reported previously. Mean age at dystonia onset was 31.3 years (range, 7 to 54 years). Onset was in the neck in 82% of carriers, and 93% had neck involvement at the final examination. Most carriers progressed to have dystonia at other sites, and only 46% still had focal dystonia at the last examination. Cranial involvement was present in 57% and speech involvement in 44%. No carrier had brachial onset, and only 32% eventually had arm involvement. Fuchs et al. (2013) noted that this distinguished the GNAL phenotype from DYT6. Less common sites of onset included the legs, larynx, jaw, and tongue. In 2 families (D1 and P), the probands had generalized dystonia that began in the legs, at ages 7 and 25 years.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on 2 families with autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia (families P and D1). In family P, they found a heterozygous nonsense mutation in the GNAL gene (S293X) that lay within a region of possible linkage and segregated with dystonia. In family D1, they found a heterozygous missense mutation (V137M) that segregated with the disease. The V137M mutation was not found in 572 control chromosomes. Neither mutation was present in about 3,500 European exomes in the NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project database.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) then Sanger-sequenced the entire GNAL coding region in 39 additional multiplex families with primary torsion dystonia. These families were of mixed European origin and negative for DYT1 and DYT6 mutations. Six families (19%) carried heterozygous GNAL mutations: a nonsense mutation (R21X), 2 frameshift mutations (S95fsX110 and R198fsX210), a missense mutation (E155K), an in-frame deletion of 3 amino acids (P102-V104del), and a possible splice site mutation (c.274-5T-C). None of the variants were found in dbSNP135, about 3,500 European exomes, or 572 control chromosomes. In all families with DNA available from multiple affected individuals, the mutations segregated with the disease. The V137 and E155 residues were completely conserved in GNAL orthologs. In a BRET assay of Galpha-olf coupling to the dopamine D1 receptor in HEK293 cells, the S293X mutant supported no D1R-driven responses. The V137M and E155K mutants showed intermediate phenotypes, largely consistent with impaired association with Gbeta-gamma subunits. A V16F variant found in a single control behaved like wildtype. The authors concluded that the findings suggested loss of function.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) noted that in striatal medium spiny neurons, Galpha-olf couples dopamine D1 receptors (D1R) and adenosine A2A receptors (A2AR) to the activation of adenylyl cyclase type 5. They proposed that GNAL mutations point to primary abnormalities of D1R and/or A2AR transmission as a possible cause of dystonia. Unlike the mutations in dopa-responsive dystonia, GNAL mutations would place the primary abnormality postsynaptically, in striatal dopaminoceptive neurons and/or cholinergic interneurons.

paragraphs.text: In 2 affected members of a family with primary torsion dystonia (family S), Fuchs et al. (2013) found a heterozygous c.463G-A transition in the GNAL gene, resulting in a glu155-to-lys (E155K) substitution at a completely conserved residue. In a BRET assay, the mutant showed an intermediate phenotype, largely consistent with impaired association with Gbeta-gamma subunits.

paragraphs.text: In the proband of a family with primary torsion dystonia (family N), Fuchs et al. (2013) found a heterozygous 9-bp deletion (c.304-312delCCTCCAGTT) in the GNAL gene, resulting in an in-frame deletion of 3 amino acids (P102-V104del). The proband was a man who developed focal dystonia with onset in the neck at age 20 years.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a family with primary torsion dystonia (family B), Fuchs et al. (2013) found a heterozygous c.274-5T-C transition upstream of exon 4 of the GNAL gene, which they described as a possible splice site mutation. Bioinformatic analysis suggested that the wildtype sequence was 10 times more likely than the mutant sequence to be found near an acceptor splice site. However, the authors could not test this in patient samples because GNAL expression was undetectable in lymphoblasts.
